articles.title: 😬 Researcher Pegs The Odds Of A.I. Wiping Out Humanity At 10%; The Industry Nods Thoughtfully, Then Returns To Building It As Fast As Possible
articles.dateline: SAN FRANCISCO — reported from the 90% that's going great
paras: A researcher at a leading A.I. lab offered a memorable estimate this week, suggesting there is roughly a one-in-ten chance the technology could end humanity — a figure delivered with the calm precision of a weather forecast, and received by the industry with a thoughtful nod and no change whatsoever to anyone's schedule.

"We take safety extremely seriously," the field said, of a number that would clear any building on Earth if it were printed on an elevator. Experts note the truly modern part is the percentage itself: we have reached a point where the smartest people alive will quantify the odds of the apocalypse to a decimal place, announce it publicly, and then break for lunch, secure in the knowledge that 90% is, mathematically speaking, most of the way to fine.

articles.title: 💰 Chip Firm Signs A $60 Billion Deal To Sell Servers To A Cloud Giant; The Numbers In Tech Have Officially Stopped Meaning Anything
articles.dateline: THE PRESS RELEASE — reported past the point of comprehension
paras: A major chipmaker announced an agreement to supply as much as sixty billion dollars of server hardware to a cloud giant, a sum so large it has quietly crossed the threshold beyond which human beings can no longer picture it, feel it, or meaningfully react to it beyond saying "wow, sixty billion" and moving on.

"It reflects the scale of demand," the company said, of a figure that would once have been the entire value of a large company and is now a supply contract. Analysts note the A.I. era has broken our relationship with numbers: a billion used to be a headline, sixty billion is a Tuesday, and somewhere in there the human brain simply filed the whole thing under "a lot" and went to get coffee.

articles.title: 🧵 Glassmaker To Lay 80 Million Miles Of Fiber For A.I. Networks; The Internet Is Getting A Dramatically Bigger Straw
articles.dateline: THE TRENCH — reported from beside a very long spool
paras: A century-old glass company signed a multibillion-dollar deal to supply eighty million miles of fiber-optic cable for A.I. network buildouts — enough glass thread to wrap around the planet several thousand times, all so the machines can talk to each other a little bit faster.

"Bandwidth is the bottleneck," the company said, of a plan to physically thread the Earth with enough cable to reach well past the sun. Experts note the strangely reassuring truth beneath the A.I. gold rush: for all the talk of clouds and intelligence and abstraction, the future ultimately comes down to somebody, somewhere, burying an almost unimaginable amount of very thin glass in the actual ground.

articles.title: 📈 A.I. Infrastructure Stocks Soar On A Pile Of New Deals; Wall Street Cheers The Act Of Spending Money On The Ability To Spend More
articles.dateline: THE TRADING FLOOR — reported from a very green screen
paras: Shares across the A.I. hardware world jumped after a flurry of enormous supply deals, as investors took the news that companies plan to spend colossal sums building data centers as a wonderful sign that companies will keep spending colossal sums building data centers.

"Momentum is strong," analysts said, of a market that now rises chiefly on evidence that the spending will continue. Observers note the logic has folded neatly in on itself: every announcement that someone will buy more infrastructure lifts the stocks of everyone who sells it, who use the gains to build more, which is announced, which lifts the stocks — a machine that runs on optimism about its own fuel consumption.

articles.title: 🎤 Big Conference Puts Rival A.I. Chiefs On One Stage; Everyone Who Might Accidentally End The World, Networking In A Single Room
articles.dateline: THE MAIN STAGE — reported from the very expensive front row
paras: A major tech conference announced a lineup featuring the leaders of nearly every top A.I. lab, gathering under one roof the small group of people currently racing one another to build the most powerful technology in history — plus a coffee bar and a lanyard for everyone.

"It's about the exchange of ideas," organizers said, of an event where the exchange of ideas is precisely what the attendees spend the rest of the year desperately trying to prevent among their competitors. Sociologists note the surreal spectacle of it: the handful of humans holding the industry's most consequential decisions, all shaking hands, comparing notes, and heading to the same after-party, before returning to their labs to keep the whole thing a secret from each other again.

horoscopes.text: You will hear a terrifying statistic today and then eat a perfectly nice sandwich. Both things are true. Balance, as ever, is everything.
A number too large to feel will pass through your life today. Do not try to picture $60 billion. Nobody can. Get the coffee instead.
Somewhere, 80 million miles of glass is being buried for you. You will never see it. It will carry your cat videos regardless. Be grateful.

tech_tip: When someone gives the apocalypse a percentage, remember it's an estimate, not a schedule. When someone says '$60 billion,' don't strain to picture it — just nod, like everyone else, and enjoy your sandwich.
gadget_watch: No new gadget this week — just the invisible plumbing of the future: sixty-billion-dollar server deals and eighty million miles of glass thread being stitched into the planet so your phone can load half a second faster. You're welcome. Probably.
